experiments.title: Get, inspect, close and misuse a connection
experiments.question: What does dataSource.getConnection() return, what does the driver say about itself, and what happens after close()?
experiments.claim: The DataSource returns a pool proxy over a driver connection; close() hands it back (the MySQL session stays open) and a closed connection refuses new statements.

experiments.title: DriverManager versus a pooled DataSource
experiments.question: Open and close connections with DriverManager and with the application's DataSource and ask MySQL which sessions still exist.
experiments.claim: DriverManager opens a new physical session each time and close() ends it; a pooled DataSource keeps the session open after close().

experiments.title: How the JDBC driver is found
experiments.question: Which Driver classes has DriverManager registered, and which one accepts which URL?
experiments.claim: Drivers register themselves through the service-provider mechanism; the MySQL driver accepts jdbc:mysql: URLs only.

experiments.title: SELECT with a Statement and a ResultSet
experiments.question: Execute a fixed SELECT with a Statement, walk the ResultSet and close everything.
experiments.claim: executeQuery returns a cursor over the rows; MySQL's own counter shows one SELECT received; the ResultSet and Statement report closed afterwards.

experiments.title: SELECT with a PreparedStatement and bound parameters
experiments.question: Prepare one SQL text with ? placeholders and execute it twice with different values.
experiments.claim: The SQL text holds placeholders and no values, and the same statement object is executed twice.

experiments.title: Why parameter binding stops SQL injection
experiments.question: Bind a quote-and-OR text as a parameter and compare it with the unsafe construction (explained, not run).
experiments.claim: The hostile text bound as a parameter matches no row; it is data, not SQL.

experiments.title: executeQuery, executeUpdate and execute
experiments.question: Which method fits which statement, and what does the driver say when you choose the wrong one?
experiments.claim: executeQuery returns a ResultSet, executeUpdate a row count, execute a boolean that says which one is available; a wrong choice is refused.

experiments.title: Closing statements, result sets and connections
experiments.question: What does each close() do to the other resources?
experiments.claim: Closing a Statement closes its ResultSet; a closed connection cannot be used again.

experiments.title: INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE and the row counts
experiments.question: Run each operation once with a PreparedStatement, ask for the generated key and check the rows affected.
experiments.claim: INSERT returns 1 and a generated key, UPDATE and DELETE return 1 for an existing row and 0 for a missing one, and MySQL's counters match.

experiments.title: Reading many rows
experiments.question: Read five rows and map them by hand, then ask for COUNT(*) instead.
experiments.claim: A loop over the ResultSet reads every row; COUNT(*) answers a count question with one row.

experiments.title: Batch insert
experiments.question: Send five INSERTs with addBatch and executeBatch inside one transaction and ask MySQL how many INSERTs it received.
experiments.claim: executeBatch returns one update count per statement; the rows are invisible to another connection until commit; with default driver settings MySQL still receives five INSERTs.

experiments.title: Auto-commit: every statement is its own transaction
experiments.question: Run one UPDATE on a new connection without calling commit() and read it from a second connection.
experiments.claim: With auto-commit (the JDBC default) the change is committed by itself and a second connection sees it at once.

experiments.title: Four statements, one commit
experiments.question: Turn auto-commit off, run two UPDATEs and two INSERTs, look from a second connection, then commit().
experiments.claim: The changes are invisible to the second connection until commit(); then all of them appear together, and MySQL counts one commit.

experiments.title: Four statements, one rollback
experiments.question: Do the same work and call rollback() instead of commit().
experiments.claim: rollback() discards every statement of the transaction, including ones that succeeded; no other connection ever saw them.

experiments.title: A failing statement in the middle
experiments.question: Let the second statement violate a foreign key and look at the first one before and after rollback().
experiments.claim: MySQL refuses only the failing statement; the first change stays pending in the open transaction until the code rolls back.

experiments.title: A savepoint inside a transaction
experiments.question: Set a savepoint, do more work, roll back to the savepoint and commit.
experiments.claim: Rolling back to a savepoint undoes only the later work and leaves the transaction open; the commit keeps the earlier work.

experiments.title: Isolation levels, observed with two connections
experiments.question: Read a row twice in one transaction while another connection changes it, at three isolation levels.
experiments.claim: REPEATABLE READ gives a stable snapshot, READ COMMITTED shows the other connection's committed change, READ UNCOMMITTED shows even its uncommitted change.

experiments.title: Borrow, return and reuse a pooled connection
experiments.question: Borrow the only connection of a dedicated lab pool, return it, and borrow again.
experiments.claim: close() returns the connection to the pool without ending the MySQL session, and the next borrower gets the same physical session.

experiments.title: Several connections at once
experiments.question: Borrow three connections from a pool that may grow to three and return them.
experiments.claim: Three simultaneous borrowers get three different sessions; after returning them the pool holds three idle connections.

experiments.title: Pool exhaustion and the acquisition timeout
experiments.question: Borrow every connection of a two-connection pool and ask for a third, then return one.
experiments.claim: The third request waits for the connection timeout and fails with SQLTransientConnectionException; after one connection is returned, requests succeed again.

experiments.title: JdbcTemplate against plain JDBC
experiments.question: Read the same rows with hand-written JDBC and with JdbcTemplate (RowMapper, ResultSetExtractor, queryForObject) and look at the JDBC calls the template made.
experiments.claim: JdbcTemplate returns the same rows and the captured calls show it acquired, prepared, executed and closed everything itself.

experiments.title: NamedParameterJdbcTemplate and batchUpdate
experiments.question: Insert with :named parameters, repeat a name, and run a batch update; look at the SQL the driver received.
experiments.claim: Spring rewrites :names to ? placeholders before the statement reaches JDBC, and batchUpdate returns one update count per row.

experiments.title: SQLException translation
experiments.question: Cause a duplicate key, a foreign key violation and invalid SQL through JdbcTemplate.
experiments.claim: Each MySQL error becomes a subclass of Spring's DataAccessException (DuplicateKeyException, DataIntegrityViolationException, BadSqlGrammarException) with the SQLException kept as the cause.

experiments.title: Spring's transaction abstraction over JDBC
experiments.question: Run two updates in a TransactionTemplate, once returning normally and once throwing, and look at the JDBC calls.
experiments.claim: Spring makes the same JDBC calls as hand-written transaction code (setAutoCommit(false), commit or rollback) and uses ONE connection for the whole callback.

experiments.title: Read the same row through three paths
experiments.question: Read one customer with JDBC, with JdbcTemplate and with JPA and compare the SQL each path produced.
experiments.claim: All three end as a SELECT handed to the JDBC driver and return the same row; they differ in who writes the SQL, maps the row and closes the resources.

experiments.title: Insert equivalent rows through three paths
experiments.question: Insert one customer with JDBC, JdbcTemplate and JPA, each with its own transaction handling, and compare.
experiments.claim: Each path produces one INSERT and a generated key; JDBC and Spring make the commit calls visibly, while Hibernate's commit is not observed at the JDBC boundary.

experiments.title: Hibernate runs on JDBC
experiments.question: Inside one JPA transaction ask MySQL for the session id through Hibernate and through JdbcTemplate, and look at Hibernate's connection object.
experiments.claim: Hibernate and JdbcTemplate used the same MySQL session in one transaction, an uncommitted JPA insert is visible to Spring JDBC but not to a new connection, and Hibernate's connection is an ordinary JDBC connection.

limitations: SQL shown is the text the application handed to the JDBC driver (placeholders, never bound values). That the driver was called does not prove MySQL executed it: where it matters the experiment also reads MySQL's own per-session statement counters.

A successful executeUpdate does not mean the change is committed. Each transaction experiment states, step by step, whether the transaction is open, committed or rolled back, and what a SECOND connection can see.
Every experiment works on its own temporary rows in the jdbc_lab_* tables and removes them afterwards (the number removed is reported). No SpringLab application table is read or changed.
Connection pool experiments use a dedicated bounded HikariCP pool created for the run and closed afterwards. The application's own pool is only read (counts), never changed.

MySQL Connector/J prepares statements on the client by default and does not rewrite batches unless rewriteBatchedStatements=true; the lab observes the default behaviour of this application's configuration.
Behaviour described is that of the MySQL, driver and Spring versions this application runs on; other versions or settings may differ.
